lines: Picture a real cluster. A task is about to run, and its data already sits on one specific machine.
Does the scheduler run it right there immediately, or does it sometimes wait a moment, hoping for an even better slot?
Let's see what a real session actually does, rather than guess.
I checked the locality of every single task in this session, and here's the honest answer.
Every one of them reports process local. Not node local, not rack local, process local, every time.
And the reason is almost embarrassingly simple. This session has exactly one JVM, playing both driver and the only executor there is. There's no worse slot anywhere to wait for.
Here's a real question, and I want your answer before mine.
I create an RDD with absolutely no hints. No explicit partition count, no parent RDD to inherit anything from. How many partitions does it actually end up with?
Think about what Spark could possibly base that number on, with nothing else given.
answer: It's tempting to guess some fixed small number, since nothing was specified.
But Spark falls back to a specific setting, default parallelism, and in local mode that setting has one precise definition.
It's exactly the number of cores this session was given. Nothing fixed about it at all.

lines: Measured, and it's exactly that number.
This session is local with four cores, and the bare RDD gets exactly four partitions.
Change the core count on a future run, and that number would move right along with it. Nothing else is deciding it.
One more commitment, and this one has a real trap in it.
Take that same four-partition data, and run a group by shuffle on it, no override specified at all. Does the output land on the same four partitions, or does something completely different take over?
Resist the pull of the last answer. This is a genuinely different operation.
answer: It's easy to assume the shuffle just redistributes what's already there, so surely it keeps the same four.
But spark dot sql dot shuffle dot partitions is its own separate setting, living entirely in the SQL layer, with its own default of two hundred.
It has no idea how many cores this session has. And the core count has no say over it either.

lines: Measured: two hundred, not four.
The group by writes out exactly two hundred partitions. That's the shuffle setting's own default, sitting right next to the four cores the bare RDD just confirmed a moment ago.
Two completely different numbers, from two completely different places.
Last commitment, and it's the sharpest test of all.
I set the shuffle partitions setting to eight by hand, then immediately create a brand new bare RDD. Does that fresh RDD's partition count move to eight as well, or does it hold steady at four?
If these two settings secretly share one dial underneath, this is where it would show.
answer: The natural guess is that they move together, since they both govern some notion of parallelism.
But nothing about the shuffle partitions setting reaches into how a bare parallelize call decides anything.
That path only ever asks one question: how many cores are there. The SQL shuffle setting could be anything at all, and it wouldn't matter.

lines: Measured, confirmed in both directions at once.
After that change, the group by's output moved to eight, exactly as set.
But the fresh bare RDD, created in the very same session right afterward, still came back with exactly four. Neither setting ever reaches over and touches the other.
So here's the full picture, stated precisely.
Default parallelism comes from the core count, full stop. Shuffle partitions come from their own separate SQL setting, full stop. Two knobs, two different jobs, never touching.
Everything downstream of that is its own story: where a task actually gets placed, and how several jobs share those slots once they're running.

Locality waits trade fairness for a better slot. FIFO or FAIR scheduling decides how jobs split the queue. Neither shows up on a single JVM, but both are exactly as real on a cluster with more than one.
